items.title: China-Linked Spy Campaign Uses Five New Malware Families Against Central Asian Governments
items.summary: Central Asian government bodies have been targeted in a cyberespionage operation using a compact but varied set of remote access tools. The activity, tracked as SilkParasite, relied on convincing government-themed documents and trusted Windows programs to quietly place malware on victims’ systems. The campaign appears designed for intelligence collection rather than widespread disruption. Its operators used spear-phishing emails with password-protected RAR archives, then used document macros to trigger malicious code. The lures were tailored for organizations in Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and, in one case, Georgia. Bitdefender analysts identified seven malware families in the operation, including five previously undocumented tools: DriveSilkRAT, CookiETagRAT, NomadRAT, GoginRAT, and NodeEdgeRAT. The other two families were SpiceRAT and BloodAlchemy, showing that the operation blended new development with malware linked to earlier China-nexus activity. The findings underline a growing risk for public-sector networks handling economic and diplomatic decisions. Phishing lure impersonating the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Uzbekistan (Source – Bitdefender) Rather than using one noisy implant, the actors maintained several tools, changed their supporting files between builds, and used cloud services and normal-looking traffic to make investigation harder. Bitdefender said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the cluster has a China-nexus link at medium confidence. China-Linked Spy Campaign Uses Five New Malware Families Researchers first detected the activity at a Central Asian government body around October 2025, then uncovered an operation that had been active for most of a year. The evidence includes overlap with SpiceRAT, which Cisco Talos previously linked to SneakyChef, and infrastructure associated with China Unicom. Bitdefender did not attribute SilkParasite to one specific named group, stressing that shared tools alone cannot establish control. That restraint is important for public reporting. DriveSilkRAT formed the campaign’s backbone. It used a shared Google Drive folder for commands, downloaded plugins into memory, and returned collected data through the same service. Researchers saw roughly 65 infection identifiers, although that figure is an upper bound because one computer can create more than one identifier through hardware fingerprinting. AI-generated lure (Source – Bitdefender) The remaining malware families gave operators several ways to work inside a network. CookiETagRAT concealed commands in HTTP Cookie and ETag headers, while NomadRAT and GoginRAT fetched functions only when needed. NodeEdgeRAT used a bundled Node.js runtime, and BloodAlchemy included capabilities for clipboard logging, keystroke capture, and running processes under another user’s session. The delivery chain repeatedly abused DLL sideloading, where a legitimate signed application loads a harmful library placed beside it. This same technique has appeared in an AsyncRAT sideloading campaign and makes simple file-name detections less reliable, because the visible program can be a genuine tool. Defenders Should Hunt Behavior SilkParasite shows why a low number of infections should not be mistaken for a limited threat. The group’s modular tools kept the first-stage footprint small and allowed the operators to add features later. Similar use of trusted cloud storage appeared in the C2Looper OneDrive malware update , reinforcing the need to examine suspicious activity within commonly allowed services. Researchers found traces consistent with AI-assisted coding, including leftover test functions and placeholder encryption keys, but assessed that conclusion only at medium confidence. The stronger point is operational discipline: the malware avoided conventional command servers in some cases, rotated artifacts, and used in-memory execution to reduce visible evidence. Defenders should review signed applications running from unusual staging or temporary folders, especially when an unfamiliar DLL sits beside them. Teams should also investigate outbound Google Drive connections that do not match user activity, inspect scheduled tasks, and build baselines that expose unusual links between processes and cloud services. Recent Central Asian government backdoors show that the region remains an active espionage target. Users should treat both polished and poor-quality government-themed messages with caution. Some SilkParasite lures appeared deliberately cheap and AI-generated, meaning appearance alone is no longer a useful measure of trust. Organizations should limit macros, verify unexpected password-protected archives through a second channel, and train staff to report suspicious messages before opening attachments. items.title: Microsoft Entra ID Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Exploited in the Wild
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that a critical remote code execution flaw in Entra ID, its cloud-based identity and access management platform, has already been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-69836 , was disclosed on August 20, 2026, and carries the maximum severity rating of Critical, underscoring just how dangerous this bug is for organizations that rely on Entra ID to authenticate users across Microsoft 365, Azure, and countless third-party applications. At its core, CVE-2026-69836 stems from a deserialization of untrusted data issue, classified under CWE-502. In plain terms, Entra ID’s backend was found to process specially crafted data objects without properly validating them first. When an attacker sends malicious serialized data to a vulnerable endpoint, the service can be tricked into executing arbitrary code on the network, without needing any authentication or user interaction. That combination, remote exploitation plus no login required, is precisely what pushes this bug into critical territory and explains why threat actors moved quickly to weaponize it. Because Entra ID underpins single sign-on and access control for millions of enterprise tenants worldwide, a successful compromise doesn’t stay contained. An attacker who gains code execution on the identity layer could potentially pivot into connected cloud workloads, hijack authentication tokens , or manipulate access policies across an entire organization’s Microsoft ecosystem. Entra ID Vulnerability Actively Exploited Microsoft’s Security Response Center has explicitly marked this vulnerability as exploited, even though it was not publicly disclosed before the advisory dropped. That distinction matters to defenders: this wasn’t a bug hunted down by independent researchers and leaked ahead of a patch; it was discovered because Microsoft’s own telemetry or incident response teams caught real-world attack activity targeting Entra ID infrastructure. The company has not released a formal exploitability index score, labeling it “N/A,” but the confirmed in-the-wild exploitation alone should put every security team on alert. Unlike traditional CVEs that demand urgent patch deployment, CVE-2026-69836 falls into Microsoft’s cloud service CVE category. Since Entra ID is a fully managed cloud platform, Microsoft has already rolled out the fix on its own infrastructure. There are no update packages, KB articles, or configuration changes for customers to apply. Microsoft says this disclosure exists purely for transparency, giving security teams visibility into threats that touched their environment even though the fix was applied server-side before most organizations even knew the flaw existed. This approach is part of Microsoft’s broader “Toward Greater Transparency” initiative for cloud service vulnerabilities, which aims to keep customers informed about backend security incidents that previously might have gone unreported since no customer patching was involved. Microsoft credited security researcher Robert Fitzpatrick for reporting the issue through coordinated disclosure. While no direct remediation steps exist for customers, this incident is a reminder to review Entra ID sign-in logs , conditional access policies, and privileged role assignments for any signs of anomalous activity dating back to before the fix was deployed. Organizations should also treat this as a cue to tighten monitoring around identity infrastructure generally, since deserialization flaws in authentication services remain an attractive and high-impact target for sophisticated threat actors. items.title: Choosing the Right Detection Approach
items.summary: This article was co-authored by Gary Katz and Jason Deyalsingh In the prior article , we examined how Visibility, Detections, the Environment, and Threat Intelligence can each serve as starting points for identifying new detection opportunities, as well as how they can be used to filter and prioritize the detections worth pursuing. Having identified an opportunity, the next question is how best to detect it. This follow-on article delineates the different detection capabilities available to detection engineers, providing a framework for evaluating which technique is most appropriate for a given activity. There is no clear-cut answer. Different detection techniques require different types of data and levels of effort, while offering different tradeoffs in robustness, coverage, and complexity. Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain primarily focuses on atomic indicators and signatures, but today’s detection engineering discipline encompasses a much wider range of techniques for identifying malicious activity. The goal of this article is not to provide in-depth instruction on any one technique, but rather to provide detection engineers with an overview of the tools available in their toolbox, along with their strengths, limitations, and data requirements. By understanding the options available, detection engineers can make more informed decisions about which tool is best suited to the task at hand, rather than defaulting to the approach they know best. This article is also not specifically about the use of GenAI. While GenAI can support detection engineering at multiple points in the process, it does not fundamentally change the process itself; rather, it changes how that process can be implemented. We will start by grouping detections efforts into two categories: Malicious Activity: What have we seen the adversary previously do which might be applicable to our organization? Unexpected Activity: What should our systems or software be doing and what would be deemed unusual and potentially malicious These categories can be further divided into separate types of detections or activities, each of which require varying levels of effort and resources. Below we will introduce these types and identify their advantages and limitations. Then we will provide a mapping between the detection types and what source data is usually the impetus for creating them. Malicious Activity: Tool-Based Detections: These are detections usually based upon a malware signature, or network signature. These detections are mostly divorced from the procedure the adversary is performing and instead focus on the bespoke tool used by the adversary. While still important, they become less effective as adversaries have migrated more to living off the land and AI reduces the cost for building unique capabilities. In the prior article, we examined how Visibility, Detections, the Environment, and Threat Intelligence can each serve as starting points for identifying new detection opportunities, as well as how they can be used to filter and prioritize the detections worth pursuing. Having identified an opportunity, the next question is how best to detect it. This follow-on article delineates the different detection capabilities available to detection engineers, providing a framework for evaluating which technique is most appropriate for a given activity. There is no clear-cut answer. Different detection techniques require different types of data and levels of effort, while offering different tradeoffs in robustness, coverage, and complexity.

Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain primarily focuses on atomic indicators and signatures, but today’s detection engineering discipline encompasses a much wider range of techniques for identifying malicious activity. The goal of this article is not to provide in-depth instruction on any one technique, but rather to provide detection engineers with an overview of the tools available in their toolbox, along with their strengths, limitations, and data requirements. By understanding the options available, detection engineers can make more informed decisions about which tool is best suited to the task at hand, rather than defaulting to the approach they know best. This article is also not specifically about the use of GenAI. While GenAI can support detection engineering at multiple points in the process, it does not fundamentally change the process itself; rather, it changes how that process can be implemented.

We will start by grouping detections efforts into two categories:

  1. Malicious Activity: What have we seen the adversary previously do which might be applicable to our organization?
  2. Unexpected Activity: What should our systems or software be doing and what would be deemed unusual and potentially malicious

These categories can be further divided into separate types of detections or activities, each of which require varying levels of effort and resources. Below we will introduce these types and identify their advantages and limitations. Then we will provide a mapping between the detection types and what source data is usually the impetus for creating them.

In the example above we identified by the postcondition any procedure an adversary would take to change the Windows Registry Run key for persistence, but a similar could be achieved without generating a RegistryEvent by simply replacing an existing executable referenced by a Windows Registry Run key.

Limitations:

  • It may be possible for the adversary to avoid the expected pre or post condition.
  • The pre or post conditions may not be well defined or observable
Behavior-Based Detections:

These detections identify behaviors or patterns of activity associated with adversary activity. The individual behaviors may not be inherently malicious or may not be required to perform the malicious activity, but when considered in the aggregate, they can provide a valuable indication of malicious activity. These detections may look for specific actions performed in a specific order or could identify when an aggregate of micro-behaviors cross a threshold.

  • Higher false positive rate

With this in mind, it is reasonable to develop detection strategies around changes to critical configurations, specifically the changes that might relax the preventative controls within the environment.

Limitations:

  • Requires deconfliction with legitimate configuration changes

It is easy to get tunnel vision when creating detections day in and day out. Taking a step back and evaluating what you want to detection, as defined in our previous article, is a good first step. Identifying which detection approach to use can be equally important. items.summary: This article was co-authored by Gary Katz and Jason Deyalsingh Recent studies have shown that genAI is commoditizing the creation of detection rules. This elevates the minimal qualifications of the detection engineer from simply creating detections to identifying where to focus efforts, implementing more robust detection capabilities and performing the research and tooling to support them. This article will focus on the first of these skillsets, identifying opportunities to create detections which align to your organization’s needs. In the previous article, Critical Asset Analysis for Detection Engineering , we looked at one approach for prioritizing tasking for a detection engineering team. In this article, we will expand upon that analysis to examine four information sources of detection engineering and how they each can be either a starting point or a filter mechanism for prioritization. In the follow on article, we will identify different detection approaches, their limitations, and their data sources. This provides a guide for starting either from the data source perspective or from the detection mechanism perspective to prioritize tasking which aligns to your organization, skillset or detection capabilities. Teams should take a balanced approach across each of these options, using the right tool in the toolbox to achieve their goal. In general, there are four information sources or categories of inputs to consider when building out a detection. Visibility: These are the logs or events which we build the detection from. We can consider the logs currently ingested into your SIEM, EDR, etc. The logs which are not ingested but could, and logs which we could have our custom software create. (When considering the third group, keep in mind the time or effort required to have your software team respond to your request) Detections: What existing detections does the team have or what third party detections can the team repurpose for their need? Environment: What is the infrastructure, network, systems, operating systems, individuals, etc. which you are protecting? Threat Intelligence / Research: Within this article, we cover the differences and value of strategic, operational and tactical threat intelligence. Our most relevant threat intelligence is as anything which tells us about how the adversary has previously implemented a procedure or how an adversary could implement a procedure. The information might come from a 3rd party threat intelligence source, internal forensic analysis of previous attacks, or research into how an attack has previously been, or could be, performed. These four sets of data can be used to determine the importance of building a detection, the effort required to build it and the potential robustness of the resulting detection. Your analysis will most likely start with one of these four categories and pivot to the others. Let’s consider each starting point and the value and limitations associated with the approach. In each case we start with gathering that type of information and then filtering down what is important based on the other three categories of data. This allows the analyst to then pivot or research to identify the additional knowledge required to create the detection. Starting with Visibility: As mentioned above, visibility is your access to events or logs which are the basis for building detections. In some circumstances, these events were created explicitly for detecting malicious activity and thus can be an easy starting point for building detections. One resource is Microsoft’s documentation which commonly provides guidance on events-to-monitor for specific infrastructure. For example, if you were tasked to protect Active Directory, one valid place to start would be examining what events Microsoft has provided specifically for that purpose . Thus, we are starting with which events would easily provide detection opportunities, informed by our environment / infrastructure. We can then use our existing detection capabilities and intel into techniques used by our adversaries to help prioritize whether to create new detections based upon this information. Example Filters: Environment: Which of the events are applicable to the network, software, platforms, etc. and how can detections based on them be tuned to not overlap with non-malicious activity Threat Intelligence: How do the events align to expected malicious activity? What types of attacks have been recently performed against the systems these events provide visibility for? Detections: What is the gap or overlap between what this visibility allows you to detect and the existing detections. Can they be made more robust? Will this visibility provide a different way to detect the activity and therefore provide additional detection-in-depth? Once we have used the filters to inform where to prioritize our detection engineering efforts, we can begin researching the information required to build the detection. Creating a robust detection is outside the scope of this article, but many of the same data sources will inform this work. For example, detections created by third parties may provide starting points for your own detections. The intelligence, or red-team information, should provide additional details on how adversaries have previously implemented the attack. Starting with Detections: Plenty of open-source detection repositories available. SIGMA is the most well-known but github contains many repositories maintained by single users, or commercial SIEM vendors. In addition, some websites are devoted to detection-sharing. While SIGMA is designed to transform detections from their common format to specific rule engines, many genAI tools can perform a similar function, easing the reuse across providers. The difficulty here is not in finding detections, it’s in finding which detections to use. In this approach, we may start by tracking updates in repositories that prioritize quality over quantity. We then can filter by our environment, adversaries and existing detections to determine which updates are applicable and align with our visibility. While this can seem arduous, a simple agentic loop can perform the initial triage for your team, removing much of the daily burden. This triage step only identifies potential detections to use by your organization. Nothing is truly free though, additional steps still remain to tune the detection and integrate it with your detection landscape. Example Filters: Threat Intelligence: Which adversaries that target environments or organizations similar to your own use the associated malicious procedures that are identified by these detections. Visibility: Does the organization have the necessary events or logs for the detections to work? Environment: Does the detection align to the environment which you are focused on protecting? Starting with Environment: In the article mentioned above, ‘Critical Asset Analysis for Detection Engineering’, we look at protecting critical assets, but one limitation of this approach is that many organizations either do not know what their critical assets are or do not distinguish between which assets are more important to protect. We can still use the approach, even without identifying our critical infrastructure by applying it to broader types of infrastructure, for example, building detections for your exchange server, or LLM coding agents. There’s no exact approach for prioritizing what infrastructure to focus on, but a good start is to look at what infrastructure is important to your organization but is not protected by existing detections or third-party capabilities. (Starting with Infrastructure, filtering by existing detection capabilities) For example, your organization might have a large deployment of windows devices, but writing detections for a technique such as process hollowing can be lower priority since your EDR provider should identify those attacks. Instead, POS devices might also be prevalent but a current blind-spot in your detection capability. Once we determine what infrastructure to focus on, we can examine the software, threat models, etc. to identify what types of attacks are relevant. Separately, we identify what types of telemetry we currently ingest, or could ingest, to provide visibility. This telemetry could be used to identify known malicious activity or more generally identify indications of malicious activity by profiling the environment system, software, user type, etc. and then identifying anomalies in their activity. In some circumstances the DE may not find sufficient or any telemetry useful for detecting malicious activity. In this circumstance, it is the responsibility of the DE to create the events required to build detections to identify malicious activity in the environment. A great example occurring today are the eventing capabilities being developed to provide visibility into agentic tooling. DEs started with how do I detect malicious activity in a genAI agentic capability, identified the lack of visibility and built capabilities to fill that gap. Filtered by: Threat Intelligence: How do adversaries achieve these objectives in other circumstances and how can those techniques or procedures be adapted to this environment? Additionally, which threat actors are actively targeting companies that match your company’s profile. Detections: What is the gap between existing detections and new ones? How can existing detections be updated, or how can logging from the environment (for example, custom software) be updated to align to work with existing detections? Visibility: How can the identified malicious activity be identified based upon the visibility? How can the environment’s (ex: custom software) logs be updated to provide the necessary visibility? Starting with Threat Intelligence: Threat intelligence is often the starting point for developing a new detection, yet many reports contain surprisingly few actionable insights that can be translated into detection logic. This is partially because a large portion of threat intelligence is not designed for that purpose. There are three types of threat intelligence which are worth quickly reviewing to distinguish their individual value. Strategic reporting focuses on high level business risks and trending. For example, the yearly investigations or breach report from most large cyber security or infrastructure providers. This reporting can help determine where to focus but will not provide details on what to do. The report might state, ‘This year we are seeing a larger influx of ransomware attacks bypassing two-factor authentication’. It is not giving you direct data to write a detection on, but your team probably wants to review two-factor bypass methods and ensure you have detections in place to identify them. Operational threat intel focuses on the adversaries, what campaigns they are conducting, who those campaigns are targeting and what TTPs they are using. This data is commonly used for tactic and technique prioritization in detection engineering. Identify which threat actors target your industry (or have previously targeted your company directly) and focus on the techniques used by those adversaries. Prioritize reviewing reporting about new campaigns from these adversaries and build detections around the tactical intelligence associated with the intel. Tactical intel should describe how the adversary is executing their attacks. In many cases the reporting will include the IPs, domains, hashes associated with the attacks While these still provide value, they are usually not the data required for a robust detection. One reason why it is difficult to find good threat intelligence in which to build your detections is that a large portion of tactical intelligence focuses on atomic indicators or procedure-instance information. Many open-source threat intelligence articles concentrate on what they saw, vs. deeper analysis into how the individual procedures within the attack are conducted. This provides a starting point for creating your detection but may require additional internal research or combining information from across sources to create a robust detection. The open-source repository, Tired-Labs , is an example of deeper analysis of how specific techniques can be implemented by an adversary and the events required to identify them. There is a second type of tactical threat intelligence which commonly is discussed separately but we will include here, red-team articles. Red-team documentation explains how to perform an attack and usually provides example commands or code for tools. This information can provide that next-level detail that is sometimes missing from basic intelligence reporting. Now that we have defined these distinct types of threat intelligence, let’s examine how they become starting points for creating new detections. Starting Point: Strategic Threat Intelligence Filtered by: Operational Threat Intelligence: How aligned is the strategic intelligence to my organization based upon which adversaries are targeting my organization or similar types of organizations? Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity? Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity? Environment: Does the strategic intelligence align to the infrastructure we are trying to protect? Starting Point: Operational Threat Intelligence: Filtered by: Tactical Threat Intelligence: How do these new campaigns or changes in relevant threat actor activity differ from our existing knowledge of their procedures? Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity? Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity? Environment: Are these campaigns or actors targeting the infrastructure we are trying to protect? Tactical / Red-Team Threat Intelligence: Filtered by: Strategic and Operational Threat Intelligence: Does this malicious procedure align to the adversaries currently targeting my organization or align to the types of attacks commonly being performed right now? Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity? Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity? Environment: Do these malicious procedures align to the infrastructure we are trying to protect? It can be tempting to continuously identify new tactical threat intelligence which address gaps in coverage, build new detections and repeat. Work is being performed, detections are being created, gaps are being filled. But there is a reason why Strategic and Operational threat intelligence exists and there is a reason why we focused on threat intelligence last as a starting point. Attempting to respond to every piece of threat intelligence can lead to burnout without understanding if you are making a meaningful impact on your organization’s defenses, just as blindly converting every detection from an open-source repository would be unsustainable as well. Analysts are continuously bombarded on social media or threat intel sites with new flashy headlines, and it will get worse as AI both increases the attacker’s ability to build new capabilities and for articles about those attacks to be written. Some of this intelligence is crucial and must be quickly responded to, but the reporting must also be filtered to what is relevant to your organization and prioritized against other efforts which could lead to a more sustainable defense. For each category of input, we started with a primary type of information and used the other types to filter or prioritize whether that data should be used to create a detection. In practice, you will continuously pivot between these data sources as you gain additional knowledge. In the second part of this article, we will provide an alternative mapping, starting with the type of detection you wish to create and mapping it to the types of sources which would inform that detection type.   2. Detections: What existing detections does the team have or what third party detections can the team repurpose for their need?
  3. Environment: What is the infrastructure, network, systems, operating systems, individuals, etc. which you are protecting?
  4. Threat Intelligence / Research: Within this article, we cover the differences and value of strategic, operational and tactical threat intelligence. Our most relevant threat intelligence is as anything which tells us about how the adversary has previously implemented a procedure or how an adversary could implement a procedure. The information might come from a 3rd party threat intelligence source, internal forensic analysis of previous attacks, or research into how an attack has previously been, or could be, performed.

These four sets of data can be used to determine the importance of building a detection, the effort required to build it and the potential robustness of the resulting detection. Your analysis will most likely start with one of these four categories and pivot to the others. Let’s consider each starting point and the value and limitations associated with the approach.

In each case we start with gathering that type of information and then filtering down what is important based on the other three categories of data. This allows the analyst to then pivot or research to identify the additional knowledge required to create the detection.

Starting with Visibility:

As mentioned above, visibility is your access to events or logs which are the basis for building detections. In some circumstances, these events were created explicitly for detecting malicious activity and thus can be an easy starting point for building detections. One resource is Microsoft’s documentation which commonly provides guidance on events-to-monitor for specific infrastructure.

For example, if you were tasked to protect Active Directory, one valid place to start would be examining what events Microsoft has provided specifically for that purpose.

Thus, we are starting with which events would easily provide detection opportunities, informed by our environment / infrastructure. We can then use our existing detection capabilities and intel into techniques used by our adversaries to help prioritize whether to create new detections based upon this information.

Example Filters:

Environment: Which of the events are applicable to the network, software, platforms, etc. and how can detections based on them be tuned to not overlap with non-malicious activity

Threat Intelligence: How do the events align to expected malicious activity? What types of attacks have been recently performed against the systems these events provide visibility for?

Detections: What is the gap or overlap between what this visibility allows you to detect and the existing detections. Can they be made more robust? Will this visibility provide a different way to detect the activity and therefore provide additional detection-in-depth?

Once we have used the filters to inform where to prioritize our detection engineering efforts, we can begin researching the information required to build the detection. Creating a robust detection is outside the scope of this article, but many of the same data sources will inform this work. For example, detections created by third parties may provide starting points for your own detections. The intelligence, or red-team information, should provide additional details on how adversaries have previously implemented the attack.

Starting with Detections:

Plenty of open-source detection repositories available. SIGMA is the most well-known but github contains many repositories maintained by single users, or commercial SIEM vendors. In addition, some websites are devoted to detection-sharing. While SIGMA is designed to transform detections from their common format to specific rule engines, many genAI tools can perform a similar function, easing the reuse across providers. The difficulty here is not in finding detections, it’s in finding which detections to use. In this approach, we may start by tracking updates in repositories that prioritize quality over quantity. We then can filter by our environment, adversaries and existing detections to determine which updates are applicable and align with our visibility. While this can seem arduous, a simple agentic loop can perform the initial triage for your team, removing much of the daily burden.

This triage step only identifies potential detections to use by your organization. Nothing is truly free though, additional steps still remain to tune the detection and integrate it with your detection landscape.

Example Filters:

Threat Intelligence: Which adversaries that target environments or organizations similar to your own use the associated malicious procedures that are identified by these detections.

Visibility: Does the organization have the necessary events or logs for the detections to work?

Environment: Does the detection align to the environment which you are focused on protecting?

Starting with Environment:

In the article mentioned above, ‘Critical Asset Analysis for Detection Engineering’, we look at protecting critical assets, but one limitation of this approach is that many organizations either do not know what their critical assets are or do not distinguish between which assets are more important to protect. We can still use the approach, even without identifying our critical infrastructure by applying it to broader types of infrastructure, for example, building detections for your exchange server, or LLM coding agents.

There’s no exact approach for prioritizing what infrastructure to focus on, but a good start is to look at what infrastructure is important to your organization but is not protected by existing detections or third-party capabilities. (Starting with Infrastructure, filtering by existing detection capabilities) For example, your organization might have a large deployment of windows devices, but writing detections for a technique such as process hollowing can be lower priority since your EDR provider should identify those attacks. Instead, POS devices might also be prevalent but a current blind-spot in your detection capability.

Once we determine what infrastructure to focus on, we can examine the software, threat models, etc. to identify what types of attacks are relevant. Separately, we identify what types of telemetry we currently ingest, or could ingest, to provide visibility.

This telemetry could be used to identify known malicious activity or more generally identify indications of malicious activity by profiling the environment system, software, user type, etc. and then identifying anomalies in their activity.

In some circumstances the DE may not find sufficient or any telemetry useful for detecting malicious activity. In this circumstance, it is the responsibility of the DE to create the events required to build detections to identify malicious activity in the environment. A great example occurring today are the eventing capabilities being developed to provide visibility into agentic tooling. DEs started with how do I detect malicious activity in a genAI agentic capability, identified the lack of visibility and built capabilities to fill that gap.

Filtered by:

Threat Intelligence: How do adversaries achieve these objectives in other circumstances and how can those techniques or procedures be adapted to this environment? Additionally, which threat actors are actively targeting companies that match your company’s profile.

Detections: What is the gap between existing detections and new ones? How can existing detections be updated, or how can logging from the environment (for example, custom software) be updated to align to work with existing detections?

Visibility: How can the identified malicious activity be identified based upon the visibility? How can the environment’s (ex: custom software) logs be updated to provide the necessary visibility?

Starting with Threat Intelligence:

Threat intelligence is often the starting point for developing a new detection, yet many reports contain surprisingly few actionable insights that can be translated into detection logic. This is partially because a large portion of threat intelligence is not designed for that purpose. There are three types of threat intelligence which are worth quickly reviewing to distinguish their individual value.

Strategic reporting focuses on high level business risks and trending. For example, the yearly investigations or breach report from most large cyber security or infrastructure providers. This reporting can help determine where to focus but will not provide details on what to do. The report might state, ‘This year we are seeing a larger influx of ransomware attacks bypassing two-factor authentication’. It is not giving you direct data to write a detection on, but your team probably wants to review two-factor bypass methods and ensure you have detections in place to identify them.

Operational threat intel focuses on the adversaries, what campaigns they are conducting, who those campaigns are targeting and what TTPs they are using. This data is commonly used for tactic and technique prioritization in detection engineering. Identify which threat actors target your industry (or have previously targeted your company directly) and focus on the techniques used by those adversaries. Prioritize reviewing reporting about new campaigns from these adversaries and build detections around the tactical intelligence associated with the intel.

Tactical intel should describe how the adversary is executing their attacks. In many cases the reporting will include the IPs, domains, hashes associated with the attacks While these still provide value, they are usually not the data required for a robust detection.

One reason why it is difficult to find good threat intelligence in which to build your detections is that a large portion of tactical intelligence focuses on atomic indicators or procedure-instance information. Many open-source threat intelligence articles concentrate on what they saw, vs. deeper analysis into how the individual procedures within the attack are conducted. This provides a starting point for creating your detection but may require additional internal research or combining information from across sources to create a robust detection.

The open-source repository, Tired-Labs, is an example of deeper analysis of how specific techniques can be implemented by an adversary and the events required to identify them.

There is a second type of tactical threat intelligence which commonly is discussed separately but we will include here, red-team articles. Red-team documentation explains how to perform an attack and usually provides example commands or code for tools. This information can provide that next-level detail that is sometimes missing from basic intelligence reporting.

Now that we have defined these distinct types of threat intelligence, let’s examine how they become starting points for creating new detections.

Starting Point: Strategic Threat IntelligenceFiltered by:

Operational Threat Intelligence: How aligned is the strategic intelligence to my organization based upon which adversaries are targeting my organization or similar types of organizations?

Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Environment: Does the strategic intelligence align to the infrastructure we are trying to protect?

Starting Point: Operational Threat Intelligence:Filtered by:

Tactical Threat Intelligence: How do these new campaigns or changes in relevant threat actor activity differ from our existing knowledge of their procedures?

Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Environment: Are these campaigns or actors targeting the infrastructure we are trying to protect?

Tactical / Red-Team Threat Intelligence:Filtered by:

Strategic and Operational Threat Intelligence: Does this malicious procedure align to the adversaries currently targeting my organization or align to the types of attacks commonly being performed right now?

Detections: What gaps do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Visibility: What visibility do we have in identifying this type of activity?

Environment: Do these malicious procedures align to the infrastructure we are trying to protect?

It can be tempting to continuously identify new tactical threat intelligence which address gaps in coverage, build new detections and repeat. Work is being performed, detections are being created, gaps are being filled. But there is a reason why Strategic and Operational threat intelligence exists and there is a reason why we focused on threat intelligence last as a starting point. Attempting to respond to every piece of threat intelligence can lead to burnout without understanding if you are making a meaningful impact on your organization’s defenses, just as blindly converting every detection from an open-source repository would be unsustainable as well. Analysts are continuously bombarded on social media or threat intel sites with new flashy headlines, and it will get worse as AI both increases the attacker’s ability to build new capabilities and for articles about those attacks to be written. Some of this intelligence is crucial and must be quickly responded to, but the reporting must also be filtered to what is relevant to your organization and prioritized against other efforts which could lead to a more sustainable defense.

For each category of input, we started with a primary type of information and used the other types to filter or prioritize whether that data should be used to create a detection. In practice, you will continuously pivot between these data sources as you gain additional knowledge. In the second part of this article, we will provide an alternative mapping, starting with the type of detection you wish to create and mapping it to the types of sources which would inform that detection type.

Next we examine Choosing the Right Detection Approach
